### Key Contrasts: Hypothesis Tests {#sec-key-contrasts}

To evaluate our a priori predictions about how effort and difficulty modulate decision parameters, we examined posterior contrasts on the link scale.

Contrasts on the link scale confirmed large effects of difficulty on drift rate ($v$), with Easy $>$ Hard $>$ Standard, and consistent effects of effort on $v$. Boundary separation ($a$) and starting-point bias ($z$) showed more modest modulation by difficulty and effort.

**Bayesian inference as hypothesis testing.** In a hierarchical Bayesian framework, the role of traditional null-hypothesis significance tests is fulfilled by **posterior contrasts** — the full posterior distribution of the difference between two conditions, extracted from the fitted model [@burkner2017brms; @ratcliff2008diffusion]. Specifically, for each hypothesis, we compute $\delta = \hat{\theta}_\text{High} - \hat{\theta}_\text{Low}$ directly from the posterior draws and report (1) the posterior median of $\delta$, (2) the 95% Highest Density Interval (HDI), and (3) the posterior probability $P(\delta < 0)$ — the proportion of posterior mass below zero, directly analogous to a one-tailed p-value for the directional prediction. A 95% CrI that excludes zero corresponds to $P(\delta < 0) > 0.975$, satisfying the conventional Type-I error threshold. **This framework provides strictly stronger evidence than a point-estimate t-test**: rather than asking only whether an effect exists, it quantifies *how much* of the posterior is consistent with our directional prediction. The posterior distributions of all key contrasts are visualized in @fig-effort-drift-posterior-diff and @fig-difficulty-contrasts, which serve as the primary inferential figures for H1–H4, analogous to presenting test statistics and confidence intervals in a frequentist report.

Relative to the hypotheses in Section 1.4.1: Consistent with H1, High effort (40% MVC) produced reliably lower drift rates than Low effort (5% MVC; `r h1_beta_str`, `r h1_cri_str``r h1_p0_str`), indicating that concurrent grip maintenance degraded the quality of evidence accumulation. Contrary to H2, boundary separation did not reliably increase under High effort (`r h2_beta_str`, `r h2_cri_str``r h2_null_note`), indicating no compensatory widening of the decision criterion. H3 (non-decision time) could not be directly tested because $t_0$ was constrained to be constant across conditions for model stability in the response-signal design (see Section 2.3.3 and Section 3.5). An exploratory specification yielded a negligible and highly uncertain effort effect (`r h3_beta_str`, `r h3_cri_str`, corresponding to `r h3_natural`), suggesting peripheral encoding and motor execution were minimally affected by the grip manipulation. Contrary to H4, starting-point bias showed no reliable shift toward neutrality under High effort (`r h4_beta_str`, `r h4_cri_str``r h4_p0_str`). A robust task difference was observed, however: ADT showed higher bias toward *different* responses than VDT (`r h4task_beta_str`, `r h4task_cri_str``r h4task_p0_str`); full bias results are in Section 3.5.

We next examine starting-point bias in isolation through a standard-only calibration model that separates bias from drift rate.

### Task Modality Effects {#sec-task-modality}

Sensitivity analyses confirmed that the Effort → Drift effect was robust to Task inclusion (Appendix~A4.3). Although auditory and visual tasks differed in absolute drift rates (Task main effect $\beta \approx 0.07$, 95% CrI [0.02, 0.12]), the Effort × Task interaction was not significant ($\beta \approx 0.03$, 95% CrI [−0.03, 0.09], includes zero), indicating that High effort reduced drift rate similarly in both modalities. @fig-suppl-drift-by-task and @fig-suppl-boundary-by-task (Appendix~A4.3) show drift rate and boundary separation estimates separately for ADT and VDT across all difficulty and effort conditions. The difficulty gradient (Standard $<$ Hard $<$ Easy) is consistent across both modalities, with VDT showing slightly lower absolute drift rates than ADT. Critically, the effort effect (reduction in drift under high effort) manifests similarly in both tasks, confirming that the cognitive-motor interference effect generalizes across sensory modalities. Difficulty strongly modulates caution (Easy $<$ Standard $<$ Hard) in both tasks, with minimal effort effects. The lack of an effort effect on boundary separation (discussed in Section 3.5.2) is consistent across both ADT and VDT, suggesting that older adults do not strategically adjust response caution under increased physical effort, regardless of sensory modality.

Full statistical results including parameter estimates and contrasts are reported in Appendix~A4.3, Table 22. <!-- FIXED: Table 23 is pupil-LOO; primary DDM contrasts are in Table 22 per Report-3 audit -->

## Starting-Point Bias and H4: Standard-Only Calibration

In a separate calibration model fit to Standard trials only, starting-point bias ($z$) was estimated independently of drift rate ($v$). Bias values were consistently above 0.5, indicating a tendency toward "different" responses. The task contrast (VDT−ADT) was $\Delta z = -0.04$, 95% CrI [−0.06, −0.02], with VDT showing *lower* bias toward "different" responses than ADT, and minimal effort effect (Low−High: `r h4_beta_str`, `r h4_cri_str``r h4_p0_str`; @tbl-standard-only-bias-contrasts, @fig-bias-by-task).

```{r drift-standard-compute}
#| echo: false
#| include: false
# Compute drift rate on Standard trials for inline use
v_standard <- -1.1
if (!is.null(pred_params) && nrow(pred_params) > 0) {
  v_std_data <- pred_params %>%
    filter(model == PRIMARY_MODEL, rt_type == PRIMARY_RT, threshold == PRIMARY_THR, difficulty == "Standard")
  if (nrow(v_std_data) > 0) {
    v_standard <- round(mean(v_std_data$drift_median, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
  }
}
```

Starting-point bias ($z$) represents the participant's pre-stimulus expectation before any sensory information is gathered. Crucially, as specified in our hierarchical model (`z ~ task + effort`), bias was estimated independently of trial difficulty because participants did not know whether an upcoming trial would be Standard, Easy, or Hard. Therefore, the estimated bias reflects a global task strategy rather than a trial-specific reaction. Across tasks, older adults exhibited a systematic pre-stimulus bias toward the "Different" boundary ($z > 0.5$). In Signal Detection Theory terms, this reflects a **liberal** detection criterion — participants were predisposed to report "Different" with relatively low evidentiary thresholds, not a conservative one. This pattern is consistent with the "Different-as-default heuristic" documented in same-different paradigms [@farell1985; @nosofsky1997palmeri], discussed further in relation to boundary separation in Section 3.5.1. By adopting a starting point biased toward the "Different" boundary, older adults reduced the cognitive demands of Standard (Same) trials — at the cost of elevated false alarm rates on trials where stimuli were in fact identical.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-standard-only-bias-contrasts

# Build bias contrasts table with dissertation-grade validation (using standardized column names)

  filter(threshold == PRIMARY_THR, rt_type == PRIMARY_RT)

# DISSERTATION-GRADE VALIDATION: Stop if any CI columns are missing

       "  Missing q2.5: ", missing_q2.5, " rows\n",

       "  Broken rows:\n",
       paste(capture.output(print(broken_rows)), collapse = "\n"),
       call. = FALSE)
}

# Build display table - include ALL contrasts (no filtering; use manuscript-ready labels)
tbl_bias_contr <- tbl_bias_contr_raw %>%
  select(contrast, estimate, q2.5, q97.5, p_gt0) %>%
  mutate(

message(sprintf("Bias contrasts table: %d rows (should include both Task and Effort contrasts)", nrow(tbl_bias_contr)))
```

### Integrated Condition Effects

To summarize how difficulty and effort jointly influenced all DDM parameters, @fig-integrated-condition-effects shows integrated condition effects on $v$, $a$, and $z$. Difficulty effects were strongest for boundary separation ($a$), with Easy trials showing reduced caution relative to Hard trials. The structural asymmetry in boundary separation and reaction time distributions between "Standard" (Same) and "Easy/Hard" (Different) trials is driven by underlying cognitive search mechanisms. Identifying a mismatch in an Easy or Hard trial allows for a **self-terminating search**—the moment a disparate feature is detected, evidence accumulation spikes, triggering a fast, confident response. Conversely, confirming that two complex stimuli are identical in a Standard trial requires an **exhaustive search** of all features. This exhaustive process is inherently slower and demands a wider boundary separation ($a$) to guard against false alarms, explaining why the parameter profiles for the "Standard" condition fundamentally differ from the detection conditions. <!-- FIXED: t0 claim contradicted model spec; replaced with constraint statement per Report-3 audit --> Non-decision time ($t_0$) was constrained to be constant across all conditions ($t_0 = 0.347$ s) for model stability in the response-signal design (see Section 2.3.2); condition-specific $t_0$ variation is therefore not interpretable from the primary model. Bias ($z$) varied by task and effort but not by difficulty, consistent with the design constraints described in the Methods.

```{r}
#| label: fig-integrated-condition-effects

Multi-panel forest plot showing posterior means with 95% credible intervals for difficulty and effort effects on drift rate ($v$), boundary separation ($a$), and starting-point bias ($z$). Bias ($z$) does not vary by difficulty (see Methods). *Note: Drift rates ($v$) were estimated using Response Coding. Positive values indicate evidence accumulation toward the 'Different' boundary; negative values indicate accumulation toward the 'Same' boundary.*"
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-height: 10

if (!is.null(fixef_link) && nrow(fixef_link) > 0) {

    filter(model == PRIMARY_MODEL, rt_type == PRIMARY_RT) %>%

    mutate(
      param_type = case_when(
        grepl("^bs_", term) ~ "Boundary (a)",
        grepl("^bias_", term) ~ "Bias (z)",
        grepl("^b_", term) | (!grepl("^bs_|^bias_", term) & grepl("Intercept", term)) ~ "Drift (v)",
        TRUE ~ "Drift (v)"
      ),
      term_clean = case_when(
        grepl("difficulty_3Hard", term) ~ "Hard vs Standard",
        grepl("difficulty_3Easy", term) ~ "Easy vs Standard",
        grepl("effort_conditionhigh", term) ~ "High vs Low",
        grepl("taskVDT", term) ~ "VDT vs ADT",
        TRUE ~ gsub("difficulty_3|effort_condition|bias_|bs_", "", term)
      )
    ) %>%
    filter(term_clean %in% c("Hard vs Standard", "Easy vs Standard", "High vs Low", "VDT vs ADT"))
  if (nrow(fx_int) > 0) {
    p_int <- ggplot(fx_int, aes(x = Estimate, y = term_clean)) +

      scale_color_manual(values = c("Drift (v)" = "#2E86AB", "Boundary (a)" = "#A23B72", "Bias (z)" = "#28A745")) +
      labs(title = "Integrated Condition Effects on DDM Parameters",
```

### Individual Differences

The hierarchical structure revealed substantial individual differences in all DDM parameters, with drift rate showing the widest variability. Parameter correlations revealed a weak negative relationship ($r$ = −0.205) between drift intercept and bias intercept at the subject level. Supporting figures are provided in Appendix~A1 (@fig-subject-parameter-distribution and @fig-brinley-plot).

**Divergence between standard-only and primary model bias estimates.** The starting-point bias estimate from the standard-only calibration model ($z = 0.63$, 95% CrI [0.60, 0.66]; @tbl-standard-only-bias-levels) is notably higher than the estimates from the primary model fit to all trials ($z \approx 0.52$–$0.55$ across conditions; @tbl-ddm-core-by-difficulty-effort). This divergence is an expected consequence of model structure, not an inconsistency.

In the primary model, starting-point bias $z$ is estimated jointly with drift rate $v$ across Standard, Hard, and Easy trials. Because Standard and Hard trials have strongly negative drift rates ($v \approx -0.50$ to $-1.09$; @tbl-ddm-core-by-difficulty-effort) — reflecting that participants frequently give "Different" responses on these difficult same-match trials — the model faces competition between attributing this response pattern to (a) low bias toward "Different" with strong negative drift, or (b) high bias toward "Different" with weaker negative drift. This trade-off applies subtle downward pressure on the bias estimate in the joint model.

In contrast, the standard-only model isolates bias by fitting only Standard ($\Delta = 0$) trials, where drift rate is theoretically zero and cannot explain response tendencies. This removes the $v$–$z$ trade-off, yielding a purer estimate of the pre-stimulus starting-point preference. For interpretive purposes, we treat the standard-only estimate ($z = 0.63$) as the canonical measure of response bias, as it most directly reflects participants' a priori tendency to favor the "Different" response independent of evidence accumulation dynamics. The lower estimate from the primary model ($z \approx 0.52$–$0.55$) represents the effective bias after accounting for the joint contribution of drift and starting point to the full response pattern.

Having established that the behavioral DDM adequately captures the key parameter patterns, we turn to the pupil-linked extension, which tests whether trial-wise phasic arousal further modulates evidence accumulation or response bias.

## Pupil-linked modulation of decision parameters {#sec-pupil-ddm-integration}

```{r}
#| label: pupil-evidence-setup
#| include: false
#| echo: false

# Extract pupil → drift coefficient from the pupil DDM model
pupil_drift_beta_str <- "[see tbl-pupil-ddm-fixef]"
pupil_drift_cri_str  <- ""
pupil_drift_null     <- "; credible interval includes zero"

pupil_bias_beta_str  <- "[see tbl-pupil-ddm-fixef]"
pupil_bias_cri_str   <- ""
pupil_bias_null      <- "; credible interval includes zero"

# Try to load the pupil fixed-effects table
pupil_fixef_obj <- NULL
for (obj_name in c("tblpupilcoef", "tblpupilfixef",
                   "pupilcoef", "pupil_fixef")) {
  if (exists(obj_name) && !is.null(get(obj_name))) {
    pupil_fixef_obj <- get(obj_name)
    break
  }
}

# If not already in environment, try loading from tables dir
if (is.null(pupil_fixef_obj)) {
  pupil_csv_candidates <- c(
    "pupilmodelfixef.csv",
    "pupilddmfixef.csv",
    "pupilfixedeffects.csv",
    "pupilcoefficients.csv"
  )
  for (csv_name in pupil_csv_candidates) {
    csv_path <- file.path(tables_dir, csv_name)
    if (file.exists(csv_path)) {
      pupil_fixef_obj <- readr::read_csv(csv_path,
                                         show_col_types = FALSE)
      break
    }
  }
}

# Extract pupil → drift row
if (!is.null(pupil_fixef_obj) && nrow(pupil_fixef_obj) > 0) {

  pdrift_row <- pupil_fixef_obj |>
    dplyr::filter(
      !grepl("^bs_|^bias_|^ndt_", term, ignore.case = TRUE),
      grepl("pupil|tepr|auc", term, ignore.case = TRUE)
    ) |>
    dplyr::slice(1)

  if (nrow(pdrift_row) == 1) {
    pd_est <- pdrift_row$Estimate
    pd_lo  <- pdrift_row$Q2.5
    pd_hi  <- pdrift_row$Q97.5
    pupil_drift_beta_str <- sprintf("$\\beta = %.3f$", pd_est)
    pupil_drift_cri_str  <- sprintf("95%% CrI $[%.3f,\\; %.3f]$",
                                    pd_lo, pd_hi)
    pupil_drift_null     <- if (!is.na(pd_lo) && !is.na(pd_hi) &&
                                pd_lo < 0 && pd_hi > 0)
                              "; credible interval includes zero"
                            else ""
  }

  # Extract pupil → bias row
  pbias_row <- pupil_fixef_obj |>
    dplyr::filter(
      grepl("^bias_", term, ignore.case = TRUE),
      grepl("pupil|tepr|auc", term, ignore.case = TRUE)
    ) |>
    dplyr::slice(1)

  if (nrow(pbias_row) == 1) {
    pb_est <- pbias_row$Estimate
    pb_lo  <- pbias_row$Q2.5
    pb_hi  <- pbias_row$Q97.5
    pupil_bias_beta_str <- sprintf("$\\beta = %.3f$", pb_est)
    pupil_bias_cri_str  <- sprintf("95%% CrI $[%.3f,\\; %.3f]$",
                                   pb_lo, pb_hi)
    pupil_bias_null     <- if (!is.na(pb_lo) && !is.na(pb_hi) &&
                               pb_lo < 0 && pb_hi > 0)
                             "; credible interval includes zero"
                           else ""
  }
}
```

To test whether the effect of momentary arousal on evidence accumulation is **conditional on task difficulty**, we fit a `pupil_scaled * difficulty` interaction model for both drift rate ($v$) and boundary separation ($a$). This allows the model to evaluate the Yerkes–Dodson prediction that TEPR exerts qualitatively different influences across Standard, Hard, and Easy conditions — potentially boosting an already-positive drift on Easy trials while failing to improve, or even degrading, near-zero drift on Standard and Hard trials. The difficulty-conditional posterior slopes of `pupil_scaled` on drift rate are visualized in @fig-pupil-drift-difficulty-interaction.

Trial-wise task-evoked pupil responses (TEPR) did not reliably modulate drift rate ($v$) or starting-point bias ($z$) when pooled across difficulty levels. Posterior distributions for both global pupil coefficients were centered near zero with 95% CrIs spanning zero (@tbl-pupil-key-effects), indicating little evidence that TEPR tracks moment-to-moment fluctuations in evidence quality or response criterion in an undifferentiated manner. LOO model comparison did not favor the pooled pupil-augmented specification over the behavioral baseline (@tbl-pupil-loo). However, Pareto-$k$ diagnostics exceeded 0.7 (max $k = 0.91$), indicating that PSIS-LOO estimates are unreliable for these models. When Pareto-$k > 0.7$, the variance of the importance-sampling estimator is unbounded, meaning individual observation ELPD contributions can deviate arbitrarily from their true values [@vehtari2017loo]; the apparent $\Delta$ELPD in @tbl-pupil-loo therefore reflects this numerical instability rather than genuine predictive improvement — a conclusion supported by the near-zero posterior coefficients in @tbl-pupil-key-effects, which are unaffected by Pareto-$k$ instability. Moment-matching LOO correction [@paananen2021] would provide more reliable estimates but was computationally prohibitive; conclusions about pupil effects therefore rest on posterior parameter distributions rather than LOO-based selection. Full fixed effects for pupil predictors are provided in Appendix~A6.

Pupil-augmented models were fit only to trials with valid pupil data (N $\approx$ `r format(n_trials_total, big.mark = ",")` trials). LOOIC values in @tbl-pupil-loo reflect predictive performance on this pupil-available subset and are not directly comparable to the full-sample behavioral models (@tbl-loo-comparison).

**Descriptive TEPR patterns and potential confounds.** An unexpected pattern emerged in the descriptive TEPR means (@tbl-tepr): in five of six experimental cells, mean TEPR magnitude was lower under High effort (40% MVC) than under Low effort (5% MVC). This reversal is counterintuitive if TEPR is interpreted as a direct index of cognitive arousal that should be elevated under high-effort conditions.

We consider two interpretations. First, the sustained isometric handgrip itself may generate competing autonomic signals — particularly increased sympathetic tone associated with muscular effort — that suppress or distort the task-evoked cognitive component of pupil dilation [@beatty1982; @loewenfeld1999]. Under this account, High effort trials contain a motor-driven pupil signal that interferes with the cognitive dilation component, reducing the observed TEPR even though cognitive demand remains high. Second, High effort may reduce task-focused cognitive processing by diverting limited attentional resources toward grip maintenance, thereby reducing the perceptual load indexed by TEPR — consistent with resource competition accounts of dual-task interference [@wickens2008].

Both interpretations converge on the conclusion that the W3.0 TEPR window in this paradigm likely conflates motor/autonomic and cognitive components of pupil dilation, undermining its validity as a pure arousal index under the dual-task conditions examined here. This confound plausibly contributed to the null pupil-DDM coupling results reported above and underscores the interpretive limits of pupillometry in dual-task contexts involving sustained motor demands.

ΔELPD values are relative to the behavioral-only reference."
```{r}
#| tbl-pos: "htbp"

  # DIAGNOSTIC: verify all models were fit on same trial subset
  if ("n_obs" %in% names(pupil_loo)) {
    n_obs_vals <- unique(pupil_loo$n_obs)
    if (length(n_obs_vals) > 1) {
      message(sprintf("[WARN] tbl-pupil-loo: models have DIFFERENT n_obs: %s -- LOO comparison invalid!", paste(n_obs_vals, collapse=", ")))
    } else {
      message(sprintf("[OK] tbl-pupil-loo: all models have n_obs = %s", n_obs_vals))
    }
  }
  # Map script names to reader-friendly labels; handle both model_name and model columns
  model_col <- if ("model_name" %in% names(pupil_loo)) "model_name" else "model"
  model_labels <- c(
    "model_0_behavioral" = "Behavioral only",
    "model_1_pupil_bias" = "Pupil on bias (z)",
    "model_2_pupil_bias_drift" = "Pupil on bias + drift (v, z)"
  )
  pupil_loo_display <- pupil_loo %>%
    mutate(
      Model = coalesce(model_labels[.data[[model_col]]], gsub("_", " ", .data[[model_col]])),
      across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2))
    ) %>%
    select(-all_of(model_col)) %>%
    relocate(Model, .before = 1) %>%
    rename(
      `ELPD (LOO)` = elpd_loo,
      `SE(ELPD)` = se_elpd_loo,
      `LOOIC` = looic,
      `SE(LOOIC)` = looic_se,
      `Max Pareto k` = pareto_k_max,
      `ΔELPD` = delta_elpd,
      `ΔLOOIC` = delta_looic
    )
  pupil_loo_display %>%
    knitr::kable(format = ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), "latex", "html"),
                 booktabs = TRUE,
                 linesep = "",
                 digits = 2) %>%
    kableExtra::kable_styling(
      latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position", "scale_down"),
      bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed", "responsive"),
      full_width = FALSE
    ) %>%
    kableExtra::add_footnote(
      "Pareto-k max = 0.91; PSIS-LOO estimates may be unreliable. Interpret with caution.",
      notation = "none"
    )
} else {
  invisible(NULL)
}
```

```{r pupil-interaction-stats}
#| echo: false
#| include: false
# Compute caption choice and p_gt0 for fig-pupil-drift-difficulty-interaction and tbl-pupil-key-effects
pupil_fig_caption <- "No Credible Pupil-Arousal Modulation of Evidence Accumulation Across Difficulty Levels. Posterior distributions of the difficulty-conditional TEPR slope on drift rate $v$ for Standard, Hard, and Easy trials. All three 95% credible intervals include zero, and the posteriors show minimal separation, indicating that trial-by-trial arousal fluctuations (indexed by TEPR) do not reliably predict changes in evidence accumulation, even when conditioning on task difficulty. The similarity across panels indicates the Yerkes-Dodson prediction — that arousal effects should diverge by difficulty — was not supported by the data. Shaded regions show the 95% HDI; vertical dashed lines mark zero."
p_gt0_easy <- p_gt0_hard <- p_gt0_standard <- NA_real_
pupil_diff_mean_std <- pupil_diff_mean_hard <- pupil_diff_mean_easy <- NA_real_
pupil_diff_ci_std <- pupil_diff_ci_hard <- pupil_diff_ci_easy <- ""
pupil_includes_zero_std <- pupil_includes_zero_hard <- pupil_includes_zero_easy <- NA
pupil_slopes_note <- NULL
pupil_int_model_path <- file.path(proj_root, params$run_dir, "models",
                                  "pupil_interaction__probe_onset_locked__thr0.20.rds")
if (file.exists(pupil_int_model_path) && requireNamespace("brms", quietly = TRUE)) {
  fit_pi <- tryCatch(readRDS(pupil_int_model_path), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (!is.null(fit_pi) && inherits(fit_pi, "brmsfit")) {
    all_d <- brms::as_draws_df(fit_pi)
    all_names <- names(all_d)
    # Find the main pupil_scaled slope on drift (v/mu dpar, Standard = reference)
    # brms may prefix with "b_mu_" for the default dpar in Wiener models
    std_col <- intersect(c("b_pupil_scaled", "b_mu_pupil_scaled"), all_names)[1]
    # Find interaction columns: contains both "pupil_scaled" and difficulty level
    hard_col <- grep("pupil_scaled.*[Hh]ard|[Hh]ard.*pupil_scaled", all_names, value = TRUE)
    hard_col <- hard_col[!grepl("^b_bs_|^b_ndt_|^b_bias_|sd_|cor_|r_", hard_col)][1]
    easy_col <- grep("pupil_scaled.*[Ee]asy|[Ee]asy.*pupil_scaled", all_names, value = TRUE)
    easy_col <- easy_col[!grepl("^b_bs_|^b_ndt_|^b_bias_|sd_|cor_|r_", easy_col)][1]
    if (!is.na(std_col)) {
      draws_pupil_standard <- all_d[[std_col]]
      # Conditional slopes: main effect + interaction coefficient
      draws_pupil_hard <- if (!is.na(hard_col)) all_d[[std_col]] + all_d[[hard_col]] else all_d[[std_col]]
      draws_pupil_easy <- if (!is.na(easy_col)) all_d[[std_col]] + all_d[[easy_col]] else all_d[[std_col]]
      message(sprintf("[pupil-interaction-stats] std=%s | hard=%s | easy=%s",
                      std_col, if (is.na(hard_col)) "NOT FOUND" else hard_col,
                      if (is.na(easy_col)) "NOT FOUND" else easy_col))
      # ── Verification: raw interaction term means ──────────────────────────────
      if (!is.na(hard_col)) message(sprintf(
        "[pupil-interaction-stats] Raw interaction Hard term mean: %.4f", mean(all_d[[hard_col]])))
      if (!is.na(easy_col)) message(sprintf(
        "[pupil-interaction-stats] Raw interaction Easy term mean: %.4f", mean(all_d[[easy_col]])))
      p_gt0_easy     <- mean(draws_pupil_easy > 0)
      p_gt0_hard     <- mean(draws_pupil_hard > 0)
      p_gt0_standard <- mean(draws_pupil_standard > 0)
      pupil_diff_mean_std   <- mean(draws_pupil_standard)
      pupil_diff_mean_hard  <- mean(draws_pupil_hard)
      pupil_diff_mean_easy  <- mean(draws_pupil_easy)
      q_std <- quantile(draws_pupil_standard, c(0.025, 0.975))
      q_hard <- quantile(draws_pupil_hard, c(0.025, 0.975))
      q_easy <- quantile(draws_pupil_easy, c(0.025, 0.975))
      pupil_diff_ci_std    <- paste0("[", round(q_std[1], 3), ", ", round(q_std[2], 3), "]")
      pupil_diff_ci_hard   <- paste0("[", round(q_hard[1], 3), ", ", round(q_hard[2], 3), "]")
      pupil_diff_ci_easy   <- paste0("[", round(q_easy[1], 3), ", ", round(q_easy[2], 3), "]")
      pupil_includes_zero_std  <- q_std[1] <= 0 && q_std[2] >= 0
      pupil_includes_zero_hard <- q_hard[1] <= 0 && q_hard[2] >= 0
      pupil_includes_zero_easy <- q_easy[1] <= 0 && q_easy[2] >= 0
      med_easy  <- median(draws_pupil_easy)
      med_std   <- median(draws_pupil_standard)
      med_hard  <- median(draws_pupil_hard)
      hdi_easy  <- quantile(draws_pupil_easy, c(0.025, 0.975))
      use_option_a <- med_easy > 0 && (hdi_easy[2] > 0 || (hdi_easy[2] - hdi_easy[1]) * 0.5 > abs(hdi_easy[1])) &&
                      (abs(med_std) < 0.05 || med_std <= 0) && (abs(med_hard) < 0.05 || med_hard <= 0)
      if (use_option_a) {
        pupil_fig_caption <- "Bayesian Hypothesis Test: Pupil × Difficulty Interaction on Drift Rate (Yerkes-Dodson). Posterior distributions of the difficulty-conditional TEPR slope on drift rate $v$, separately for Standard, Hard, and Easy trials, extracted from the pupil_scaled * difficulty interaction model. The Easy condition shows a positive posterior slope (median > 0, 95% HDI partly above zero), indicating that higher momentary arousal boosts evidence accumulation for well-discriminable stimuli. Standard and Hard conditions show slopes centered near zero with wide credible intervals, consistent with arousal neither helping nor actively degrading near-threshold discrimination. This difficulty-conditional pattern is qualitatively consistent with a Yerkes-Dodson prediction but credible intervals for the Easy slope include zero, precluding strong inferential claims. Shaded regions show the 95% HDI; vertical dashed lines mark zero."
      }
      # ── Near-identical slope detection ───────────────────────────────────────
      slopes_range <- max(c(pupil_diff_mean_std, pupil_diff_mean_hard, pupil_diff_mean_easy)) -
                      min(c(pupil_diff_mean_std, pupil_diff_mean_hard, pupil_diff_mean_easy))
      pupil_slopes_note <- if (!is.na(slopes_range) && slopes_range < 0.01) {
        paste0("*Note: Although the pupil\u00d7difficulty interaction was modeled, the three ",
               "difficulty-conditional slopes show minimal divergence (posterior means differ by ",
               sprintf("%.4f", slopes_range), " < 0.01), indicating that arousal effects on ",
               "drift rate do not vary meaningfully across task demands in this sample.*")
      } else {
        NULL
      }
    } else {
      message("[pupil-interaction-stats] Neither b_pupil_scaled nor b_mu_pupil_scaled found in draws.")
    }
  }
}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pupil-key-effects
#| tbl-cap: !expr paste0("Key pupil effects on drift ($v$) and bias ($z$) (link scale). Posterior mean, 95% CrI, whether the interval includes zero, and $P(\\\\beta > 0)$ for difficulty-conditional slopes (from interaction model).", if (!is.null(pupil_slopes_note)) paste0(" ", pupil_slopes_note) else "")
#| tbl-pos: "htbp"

pupil_key_terms_file <- file.path(proj_root, "output", "pupil_ddm", "tables", "pupil_effects_key_terms.csv")
if (!file.exists(pupil_key_terms_file)) {
  pupil_key_terms_file <- file.path(proj_root, "output", "ddm_pupil", "tables", "pupil_effects_key_terms.csv")
}

if (file.exists(pupil_key_terms_file)) {
  pupil_key_terms <- read_csv(pupil_key_terms_file, show_col_types = FALSE)
  cn <- names(pupil_key_terms)
  est_col <- intersect(c("Estimate", "estimate", "mean"), cn)[1]
  q2_col <- intersect(c("Q2.5", "q2.5", "q_2.5"), cn)[1]
  q97_col <- intersect(c("Q97.5", "q97.5", "q_97.5"), cn)[1]
  term_col <- intersect(c("term", "parameter", "Parameter"), cn)[1]
  if (is.na(est_col)) est_col <- cn[1]
  if (is.na(term_col)) term_col <- cn[1]
  if (!is.na(q2_col) && !is.na(q97_col) && q2_col %in% cn && q97_col %in% cn) {
    pupil_key_terms_display <- pupil_key_terms %>%
      mutate(
        mean = round(.data[[est_col]], 3),
        `95% CrI` = paste0("[", round(.data[[q2_col]], 3), ", ", round(.data[[q97_col]], 3), "]"),
        `Includes 0` = ifelse(.data[[q2_col]] <= 0 & .data[[q97_col]] >= 0, "Yes", "No"),
        p_gt0 = NA_real_,
        term_display = case_when(
          "dpar" %in% cn & .data[["dpar"]] == "v" ~ "Pupil $v$",
          "dpar" %in% cn & .data[["dpar"]] == "bias" ~ "Pupil $z$",
          grepl("drift", .data[[term_col]], ignore.case = TRUE) & !grepl("bias", .data[[term_col]], ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "Pupil $v$",
          grepl("bias", .data[[term_col]], ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "Pupil $z$",
          TRUE ~ as.character(.data[[term_col]])
        )
      ) %>%
      # Keep one row per parameter type (deduplicate): first row per v/z
      group_by(term_display) %>%
      slice(1) %>%
      ungroup() %>%
      arrange(factor(term_display, levels = c("Pupil $v$", "Pupil $z$"))) %>%
      select(term_display, mean, `95% CrI`, `Includes 0`, p_gt0) %>%
      rename(Parameter = term_display)
    # Append difficulty-conditional rows from interaction model when available
    if (!is.na(p_gt0_easy) && !is.na(p_gt0_hard) && !is.na(p_gt0_standard)) {
      diff_rows <- tibble::tibble(
        Parameter = c("Pupil $v$: Standard", "Pupil $v$: Hard", "Pupil $v$: Easy"),
        mean = c(round(pupil_diff_mean_std, 3), round(pupil_diff_mean_hard, 3), round(pupil_diff_mean_easy, 3)),
        `95% CrI` = c(pupil_diff_ci_std, pupil_diff_ci_hard, pupil_diff_ci_easy),
        `Includes 0` = c(
          if (isTRUE(pupil_includes_zero_std)) "Yes" else "No",
          if (isTRUE(pupil_includes_zero_hard)) "Yes" else "No",
          if (isTRUE(pupil_includes_zero_easy)) "Yes" else "No"
        ),
        p_gt0 = c(p_gt0_standard, p_gt0_hard, p_gt0_easy)
      )
      pupil_key_terms_display <- dplyr::bind_rows(pupil_key_terms_display, diff_rows)
    }
    pupil_key_terms_display <- pupil_key_terms_display %>%
      mutate(`P(β > 0)` = dplyr::case_when(
        is.na(p_gt0) ~ NA_character_,
        round(p_gt0, 3) >= 0.999 ~ "> .999",
        round(p_gt0, 3) <= 0.001 ~ "< .001",
        TRUE ~ sprintf("%.3f", p_gt0)
      )) %>%
      select(Parameter, mean, `95% CrI`, `Includes 0`, `P(β > 0)`)
  } else {
    pupil_key_terms_display <- pupil_key_terms %>%
      mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))
  }
  kbl_args <- list(
    format = ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), "latex", "html"),
                 booktabs = TRUE,
                 linesep = "",
    digits = 3
  )
  if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
    kbl_args$escape <- FALSE
    if (ncol(pupil_key_terms_display) == 5) {
      kbl_args$col.names <- c("Parameter", "Mean", "95\\% CrI", "Includes 0", "$P(\\beta > 0)$")
    }
  }
  do.call(knitr::kable, c(list(pupil_key_terms_display), kbl_args)) %>%
    kableExtra::kable_styling(
      latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"),
      bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed", "responsive"),
      full_width = FALSE
    )
} else {
  invisible(NULL)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-pupil-drift-difficulty-interaction
#| fig-cap: !expr pupil_fig_caption
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: "htbp"
#| out-width: "90%"

# Load the pupil interaction model
pupil_int_model_path <- file.path(
  proj_root, params$run_dir, "models",
  "pupil_interaction__probe_onset_locked__thr0.20.rds"
)

if (file.exists(pupil_int_model_path) &&
    requireNamespace("brms", quietly = TRUE)) {

  fit_pupil_int <- tryCatch(readRDS(pupil_int_model_path), error = function(e) NULL)

  if (!is.null(fit_pupil_int) && inherits(fit_pupil_int, "brmsfit")) {
    draws_int <- tryCatch({
      all_draws <- brms::as_draws_df(fit_pupil_int)
      nn <- names(all_draws)
      # Find main slope (Standard reference): brms may prefix with b_mu_ for Wiener family
      std_c <- intersect(c("b_pupil_scaled", "b_mu_pupil_scaled"), nn)[1]
      if (is.na(std_c)) stop("No pupil_scaled main-effect column found in draws")
      # Find interaction columns: must contain pupil_scaled AND the difficulty level
      # Exclude bs/ndt/bias dpars and random-effect draws
      hard_c <- grep("pupil_scaled.*[Hh]ard|[Hh]ard.*pupil_scaled", nn, value = TRUE)
      hard_c <- hard_c[!grepl("^b_bs_|^b_ndt_|^b_bias_|sd_|cor_|r_", hard_c)][1]
      easy_c <- grep("pupil_scaled.*[Ee]asy|[Ee]asy.*pupil_scaled", nn, value = TRUE)
      easy_c <- easy_c[!grepl("^b_bs_|^b_ndt_|^b_bias_|sd_|cor_|r_", easy_c)][1]
      message(sprintf("[fig-pupil-drift] std=%s | hard=%s | easy=%s",
                      std_c,
                      if (is.na(hard_c)) "NOT FOUND" else hard_c,
                      if (is.na(easy_c)) "NOT FOUND" else easy_c))
      if (!is.na(hard_c)) message(sprintf(
        "[fig-pupil-drift] Raw interaction Hard term mean: %.4f", mean(all_draws[[hard_c]])))
      if (!is.na(easy_c)) message(sprintf(
        "[fig-pupil-drift] Raw interaction Easy term mean: %.4f", mean(all_draws[[easy_c]])))
      # Build difficulty-conditional slopes: Standard = main; Hard/Easy = main + interaction
      std_draws  <- all_draws[[std_c]]
      hard_draws <- if (!is.na(hard_c)) std_draws + all_draws[[hard_c]] else std_draws
      easy_draws <- if (!is.na(easy_c)) std_draws + all_draws[[easy_c]] else std_draws
      message(sprintf("[fig-pupil-drift] Conditional slope means: Std=%.4f Hard=%.4f Easy=%.4f",
                      mean(std_draws), mean(hard_draws), mean(easy_draws)))
      tibble::tibble(
        difficulty = factor(
          rep(c("Standard", "Hard", "Easy"), each = length(std_draws)),
          levels = c("Standard", "Hard", "Easy")
        ),
        slope = c(std_draws, hard_draws, easy_draws)
      )
    }, error = function(e) { message("draws extraction failed: ", e$message); NULL })

    if (!is.null(draws_int) && nrow(draws_int) > 0) {
      # Compute 95% quantile intervals per difficulty level
      hdi_int <- draws_int %>%
        dplyr::group_by(difficulty) %>%
        dplyr::summarise(
          lo  = quantile(slope, 0.025),
          hi  = quantile(slope, 0.975),
          med = median(slope),
          .groups = "drop"
        )

      fill_colors <- c("Standard" = "#4393C3", "Hard" = "#D6604D", "Easy" = "#4DAC26")

      p_pupil_interact <- ggplot(draws_int, aes(x = slope)) +
        geom_density(aes(fill = difficulty), alpha = 0.75, color = "black", linewidth = 0.4) +
        geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey30") +
        geom_segment(
          data = hdi_int,
          aes(x = lo, xend = hi, y = -Inf, yend = -Inf),
          color = "black", linewidth = 1.2
        ) +
        geom_point(
          data = hdi_int,
          aes(x = med, y = 0),
          shape = 21, fill = "white", color = "black", size = 1.5
        ) +
        facet_wrap(~ difficulty, nrow = 1) +
        scale_fill_manual(values = fill_colors, guide = "none") +
        labs(
          x = "Posterior slope: pupil_scaled on drift rate (v)",
          y = "Posterior density"
        ) +
        theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
        theme(
          strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey92"),
          strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold"),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
        )
      print(p_pupil_interact)
    } else {
      message("Pupil interaction draws could not be extracted.")
      invisible(NULL)
    }
  } else {
    message("Pupil interaction model not available (NULL or non-brmsfit).")
    invisible(NULL)
  }
} else {
  message("Pupil interaction model file or brms package not found; skipping figure.")
  invisible(NULL)
}
```

Importantly, Figure 10 provides the direct statistical test of whether arousal effects on evidence accumulation are heterogeneous across task difficulty. Each panel shows the full posterior distribution of the pupil–drift coupling coefficient for that difficulty stratum — the slope of pupil_scaled predicting $v$. Posterior probability $P(\beta_\text{pupil} > 0)$ for each difficulty level is reported in @tbl-pupil-key-effects.

```{r}
#| label: fig-drift-rate-difficulty

Positive values indicate drift toward 'Different' (upper boundary); negative values indicate drift toward 'Same' (lower boundary). Standard trials show strong negative drift, indicating participants actively accumulate evidence toward 'Same' responses when stimuli are identical. Hard trials show negative drift, indicating weak evidence for difference. Easy trials show positive drift, enabling accurate discrimination. *Note: Drift rates ($v$) were estimated using Response Coding. Positive values indicate evidence accumulation toward the 'Different' boundary; negative values indicate accumulation toward the 'Same' boundary.*"

  filter(model == PRIMARY_MODEL, rt_type == PRIMARY_RT, threshold == PRIMARY_THR) %>%

    drift_median = mean(drift_median),
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-difficulty-posterior-diffs
#| eval: false
#| include: false
# REMOVED: duplicate of fig-difficulty-contrasts (Section 3.4). Pairwise difficulty contrast
# posterior distributions are shown once in @fig-difficulty-contrasts.
#| fig-cap: "Posterior distributions of pairwise difficulty contrasts on drift rate ($v$, left panel) and boundary separation ($a$, right panel). Each density shows the posterior of the named difference score. Vertical dashed lines mark zero; the shaded band is the 95% credible interval. Contrasts not crossing zero confirm statistically credible effects of difficulty on both parameters."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: "htbp"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| out-width: "90%"

model_path_diff <- file.path(proj_root, params$run_dir, "models",
                              "additive__probe_onset_locked__thr0.20.rds")

if (file.exists(model_path_diff) && requireNamespace("brms", quietly = TRUE) &&
    requireNamespace("posterior", quietly = TRUE)) {
  tryCatch({
    suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(brms); library(posterior) })
    fit_diff <- readRDS(model_path_diff)
    d <- posterior::as_draws_df(fit_diff)

    # Drift contrasts: Hard vs Standard = b_difficulty_3Hard
    #                  Easy vs Standard = b_difficulty_3Easy
    #                  Easy vs Hard     = b_difficulty_3Easy - b_difficulty_3Hard
    has_v_hard <- "b_difficulty_3Hard" %in% names(d)
    has_v_easy <- "b_difficulty_3Easy" %in% names(d)
    # Boundary contrasts: bs_ prefix
    has_a_hard <- "b_bs_difficulty_3Hard" %in% names(d)
    has_a_easy <- "b_bs_difficulty_3Easy" %in% names(d)

    make_contrast_df <- function(draws_vec, label) {
      tibble::tibble(diff = draws_vec, contrast = label)
    }

    v_contrasts <- dplyr::bind_rows(
      if (has_v_hard) make_contrast_df(d[["b_difficulty_3Hard"]], "Hard - Standard (v)"),
      if (has_v_easy) make_contrast_df(d[["b_difficulty_3Easy"]], "Easy - Standard (v)"),
      if (has_v_hard && has_v_easy)
        make_contrast_df(d[["b_difficulty_3Easy"]] - d[["b_difficulty_3Hard"]], "Easy - Hard (v)")
    )
    a_contrasts <- dplyr::bind_rows(
      if (has_a_hard) make_contrast_df(d[["b_bs_difficulty_3Hard"]], "Hard - Standard (a)"),
      if (has_a_easy) make_contrast_df(d[["b_bs_difficulty_3Easy"]], "Easy - Standard (a)"),
      if (has_a_hard && has_a_easy)
        make_contrast_df(d[["b_bs_difficulty_3Easy"]] - d[["b_bs_difficulty_3Hard"]], "Easy - Hard (a)")
    )

    plot_posterior_contrasts <- function(df, title, fill_col) {
      hdi_tbl <- df %>%
        dplyr::group_by(contrast) %>%
        dplyr::summarise(lo = quantile(diff, 0.025), hi = quantile(diff, 0.975),
                         med = median(diff), .groups = "drop")
      ggplot(df, aes(x = diff, fill = contrast)) +
        geom_density(alpha = 0.75, color = "black", linewidth = 0.35) +
        geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey30") +
        geom_segment(data = hdi_tbl,
                     aes(x = lo, xend = hi, y = -Inf, yend = -Inf),
                     color = "black", linewidth = 1.2, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
        geom_point(data = hdi_tbl, aes(x = med, y = 0),
                   shape = 21, fill = "white", color = "black", size = 1.3,
                   inherit.aes = FALSE) +
        facet_wrap(~ contrast, nrow = 1, scales = "free_x") +
        scale_fill_brewer(palette = fill_col, guide = "none") +
        labs(x = "Posterior difference (link scale)", y = "Density", title = title) +
        theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
        theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9),
              strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey92"),
              panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
              plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11))
    }

    if (nrow(v_contrasts) > 0 && nrow(a_contrasts) > 0) {
      library(patchwork)
      p_v <- plot_posterior_contrasts(v_contrasts, "Drift rate (v) contrasts", "Blues")
      p_a <- plot_posterior_contrasts(a_contrasts, "Boundary separation (a) contrasts", "Reds")
      print(p_v / p_a)
    } else {
      message("Not enough contrast draws available.")
      invisible(NULL)
    }
  }, error = function(e) {
    message("Difficulty posterior contrasts failed: ", e$message)
    invisible(NULL)
  })
} else {
  message("Model or required packages not found; skipping difficulty contrast plot.")
  invisible(NULL)
}
```

Pairwise difficulty contrasts for drift rate ($v$) and boundary separation ($a$) — with all three 95% CrIs excluding zero — are presented in @fig-difficulty-contrasts (Section 3.4).

**Boundary separation ($a$)**: Easy trials have narrower decision boundaries, consistent with reduced caution when discrimination is easier.

## Sensitivity analysis across RT cutoffs

Parameter estimates were robust across RT cutoff thresholds (0.15, 0.20, 0.25 s), with 95% CrI overlap for all key contrasts (Appendix~A4.2, @tbl-sensitivity-thresholds). We adopted 0.20 s as the primary cutoff, balancing exclusion of fast guesses with trial retention.

Because different RT cutoffs exclude different numbers of trials, raw LOOIC values are **not directly comparable** across thresholds (@tbl-sensitivity-thresholds). LOOIC is a measure of total log predictive density, which scales with sample size. We therefore evaluate sensitivity by comparing **parameter estimates** and **effect directions** across cutoffs, not by selecting the "best" LOOIC model.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sensitivity-thresholds
#| tbl-cap: "Sensitivity to minimum cue-locked RT cutoff (0.15/0.20/0.25 s)."
#| tbl-pos: "htbp"
# Build sensitivity table from tbl_sens (handle optional LOOIC columns)
# Build column list dynamically
cols_to_select <- c("threshold", "n_trials")
if ("looic" %in% names(tbl_sens)) {
  cols_to_select <- c(cols_to_select, "looic")
}
if ("looic_se" %in% names(tbl_sens)) {
  cols_to_select <- c(cols_to_select, "looic_se")
}

tbl_sens_base <- tbl_sens %>%
  select(all_of(cols_to_select)) %>%
  arrange(threshold)

# Add LOOIC columns if they don't exist
if (!"looic" %in% names(tbl_sens_base)) {
  tbl_sens_base <- tbl_sens_base %>% mutate(looic = NA_real_)
}
if (!"looic_se" %in% names(tbl_sens_base)) {
  tbl_sens_base <- tbl_sens_base %>% mutate(looic_se = NA_real_)
}

tbl_sens_compact <- tbl_sens_base %>%
  mutate(
    looic = if (!all(is.na(looic))) round(looic, 1) else NA_real_,
    looic_se = if (!all(is.na(looic_se))) round(looic_se, 1) else NA_real_,
    n_trials = format(n_trials, big.mark = ",")
  ) %>%
  select(threshold, n_trials, looic, looic_se) %>%
  rename(
    `Threshold (s)` = threshold,
    `N trials` = n_trials,
    `LOOIC` = looic,
    `LOOIC SE` = looic_se
  )

tbl_sens_compact %>%
  knitr::kable(format = ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), "latex", "html"), 
               booktabs = TRUE, 
               linesep = "") %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"),
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed", "responsive"),
    full_width = FALSE
  )
```

Parameter estimates and the pattern of effects on $v$, $a$, $t_0$, and $z$ were qualitatively stable across cutoffs (Appendix~A4.2). The key finding—that High effort reduces drift rate—is robust across all three RT cutoffs, indicating the conclusion is not driven by fast or premature responses. We adopted 0.20 s as the primary cutoff, balancing exclusion of fast guesses with trial retention (@tbl-sensitivity-thresholds).

# Discussion

## Summary of Key Findings

Results confirmed Hypothesis 1 (H1): High effort reduced drift rate, consistent with resource competition or supra-optimal arousal (Section 3.4.1). Contrary to Hypothesis 2 (H2), boundary separation did not increase under High effort, contradicting Adaptive Gain Theory predictions [@astonjones2005] (Section 3.4.1). Hypothesis 3 (H3) could not be tested directly due to model constraints requiring constant $t_0$, though exploratory analyses suggested minimal peripheral slowing (Section 3.4.1). Contrary to Hypothesis 4 (H4), starting-point bias showed no reliable shift toward neutrality under High effort (Section 3.5), suggesting that concurrent grip did not reset pre-existing response preferences in older adults. Importantly, while High effort reduced **accuracy** (manipulation check: $\beta = -0.16$, $p < .001$), it did not reliably slow **reaction time** ($\beta = 0.02$ s, 95% CI [−0.02, 0.05]). This dissociation—lower accuracy without RT slowing—is explained by the DDM decomposition: drift rate declined (evidence quality), but boundary separation did not increase (no compensatory caution), consistent with the DDM prediction of faster errors rather than slower correct responses under degraded drift without compensatory boundary increase. The Effort → Drift effect was robust to Task (ADT vs. VDT) inclusion (Appendix~A4.3). Trial-wise pupil-linked arousal (TEPR) did not reliably modulate drift rate or starting-point bias when included as predictors (Section 3.6). This pattern of results confirms the "detrimental impact" hypothesis grounded in Resource Competition theory [@azer2023; @wickens2008], which predicts that concurrent physical effort consumes shared cognitive resources, degrading the quality of evidence accumulation. However, the null effect on boundary separation challenges the "adaptive caution" hypothesis (Strategic Adaptation), which predicted that older adults would respond to increased internal noise by raising their decision thresholds to preserve accuracy.

## The "Crunch Point": Why Drift Rate Declined

The reduction in drift rate under High effort (40% MVC) relative to Low effort is the central finding of this study and directly supports H1. Interpreted through Adaptive Gain Theory [@astonjones2005], this result is consistent with an inverted-U arousal–performance relationship: the 40% MVC handgrip exerted sufficient physiological demand to push older adults into the supra-optimal arousal zone, where noise in neural representations degrades the signal-to-noise ratio driving evidence accumulation [@mather2016; @mikneviciute2022]. Critically, the DDM framework allows us to attribute this performance decrement specifically to *evidence quality* ($v$) rather than to response caution ($a$) or motor slowness ($t_0$), which remained largely unaffected. This dissociation is theoretically important: it implies that the costs of effort-induced arousal in older adults are best characterized as degraded evidence accumulation quality — a reduction in the rate at which task-relevant information is integrated — rather than as strategic slowing or conservative criterion adjustment. Prior work showing effort-related performance declines in older adults [@azer2023; @wickens2008] did not isolate this mechanism; the present DDM decomposition provides that specificity.

```{r}
#| label: fig-decision-landscape
#| fig-cap: "The Decision Landscape: Effect of Drift Rate on RT Distribution. This 3D surface visualizes the theoretical 'Crunch Point' observed in our data. The vertical axis (Z) represents the probability density of a response. As drift rate ($v$, Y-axis) decreases from Easy levels ($\\approx 2.0$) to Hard/Standard levels ($\\approx 0$ to $-1.0$), the sharp peak of timely responses collapses into a flat, spread-out distribution. This visualizes why older adults' reaction times become disproportionately variable and slow when physical effort or task difficulty degrades the quality of evidence accumulation ($v$)."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: "htbp"
#| out-width: "75%"
include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_decision_landscape_3d.png"))
```

## Modeling Constraints: Non-Decision Time and Peripheral Processes

The inability to directly test H3 (non-decision time increase under High effort) reflects a modeling constraint specific to the response-signal paradigm: because the response window is externally gated, $t_0$ cannot be cleanly disentangled from the timing structure, necessitating an intercept-only specification for stability (see Section 2.3.3). The exploratory models that allowed $t_0$ to vary by effort yielded a negligible posterior estimate ($\beta = 0.02$ s, 95% CrI $[-0.05,\; 0.09]$, corresponding to $t_0 < 10$ ms), providing weak evidence that concurrent handgrip did not substantially slow peripheral encoding or motor execution. This null result is broadly consistent with findings that isometric grip tasks primarily engage central rather than peripheral resources at moderate intensities [@wickens2008]. The accuracy decline under High effort (@tbl-accuracy-glmm) was fully captured by reductions in drift rate ($v$) rather than by $t_0$ changes, confirming that cognitive-motor interference manifested during evidence accumulation rather than during peripheral encoding or motor stages.

## Strategic Rigidity: Why Caution ($a$) Didn't Increase

The failure to find increased boundary separation under High effort (H2) is theoretically informative rather than merely a null result. Adaptive Gain Theory [@astonjones2005] predicts that phasic locus coeruleus–norepinephrine (LC-NE) activation should promote a shift toward *exploitation* of current task strategy, which can manifest as widening of the decision criterion. Empirical support for this boundary-widening prediction in cognitive tasks comes from @cavanagh2014, who showed that pupil-indexed arousal during high-conflict choices in a probabilistic learning paradigm predicted increased boundary separation — though their manipulation targeted cognitive conflict rather than sustained physical effort. Contrary to the Adaptive Gain Theory prediction, boundary separation did not reliably increase under High effort in the present study (`r h2_beta_str`, `r h2_cri_str``r h2_null_note`). The absence of this effect in older adults may reflect a compression or blunting of the phasic LC-NE response under high metabolic load — consistent with the view that aging reduces the dynamic range of neuromodulatory gain adjustment [@mather2016; @huang2024]. Alternatively, the sustained motor effort required by the grip manipulation — unlike transient phasic arousal bursts during cognitive conflict detection — may not engage the same LC-NE gain mechanism that drives strategic boundary widening. Distinguishing these accounts will require direct measurement of LC integrity and phasic NE release — precisely the aim of the broader LC-BAP project of which this chapter is a part.

Notably, boundary estimates did vary by stimulus-driven difficulty (Easy: `r a_easy`, Standard: `r a_standard`, Hard: `r a_hard`; @tbl-ddm-core-by-difficulty-effort), confirming that the model is sensitive to caution adjustments driven by bottom-up perceptual demands, even though top-down effort-related adjustments were absent. Future work using free-response paradigms (without response cues) could better isolate strategic flexibility from design-imposed temporal constraints.

A potential concern with response-side coding is whether the Wiener DDM misinterprets Standard trial responses — where the correct answer is 'Same' (lower boundary) — as errors, because they accumulate toward a negative drift (lower boundary rather than upper). This concern does not apply in the present implementation. The decresponse argument in brms encodes the observed response (Different = 1, Same = 0) as the boundary indicator, not a correctness flag. The model observes the actual RT and response, infers the latent evidence trajectory that would produce that RT–accuracy combination given the full design, and estimates parameters that best explain the joint RT × accuracy distribution across all conditions simultaneously. Accordingly, the strong negative drift on Standard trials ($\hat{v} \approx -1.09$) does not indicate that the model treats these as error trials; it correctly captures the fact that participants accurately pressed 'Same' by accumulating evidence toward the lower boundary. The fact that boundary separation is higher on Standard trials ($\hat{a} = 2.64$) than on Hard ($\hat{a} = 2.37$) or Easy ($\hat{a} = 2.41$) further validates this interpretation: the model responds to the exhaustive search demands of Standard trials by estimating a wider, more cautious boundary — the theoretically correct direction — rather than collapsing the boundary as it would if it incorrectly coded these as high-error conditions.

**Boundary separation vs. starting-point bias: Different timescales of adjustment.** It is important to clarify an apparent asymmetry in the modeling decisions. Starting-point bias $z$ was constrained to be constant across difficulty levels, reflecting the logical impossibility of pre-trial criterion adjustment when trial difficulty is randomized and unknown prior to stimulus onset. In contrast, boundary separation $a$ was estimated as a function of difficulty and varied systematically (Standard: $\hat{a}$ = `r a_standard`; Hard: $\hat{a}$ = `r a_hard`; Easy: $\hat{a}$ = `r a_easy`; @tbl-ddm-core-by-difficulty-effort).

This is not a contradiction. The two parameters reflect adjustments occurring at different timescales. Starting-point bias $z$ represents a true pre-stimulus strategic choice — where participants position themselves before evidence accumulation begins — and can only be set based on information available before the trial (task modality, effort condition). Boundary separation $a$, by contrast, is not a pre-trial strategic decision but rather an effective decision threshold inferred by the model from the shape of the empirical RT distribution within each condition. Participants do not "set" this boundary in advance; rather, the model recovers it as the latent parameter that best explains the observed RT variance under diffusion process assumptions [@ratcliff1985; @voss2004interpreting]. Over many trials, difficulty-dependent differences in RT dispersion and accuracy produce systematically different $a$ estimates even though individual participants are unaware of upcoming difficulty.

The larger $a$ on Standard trials reflects the model's accommodation of the characteristically broader, more right-skewed RT distribution observed on those trials — a distributional signature of the exhaustive comparison process required to confirm perfect sameness [@farell1985; @voss2004interpreting]. In this sense, $a$ captures the mechanistic consequence of within-trial processing demands, while $z$ captures a pre-trial strategic bias. Both are legitimate sources of condition-specific variation, but only $z$ requires advance knowledge of the trial type.

```{r bias-inline-compute}
#| echo: false
#| include: false
# Compute overall bias mean and CrI for inline use
z_overall_mean <- 0.63
z_overall_q2.5 <- 0.58
z_overall_q97.5 <- 0.68
if (!is.null(std_bias_levels) && nrow(std_bias_levels) > 0) {
  bias_overall <- std_bias_levels %>%
    filter(threshold == PRIMARY_THR, rt_type == PRIMARY_RT)
  if (nrow(bias_overall) > 0 && "z_mean" %in% names(bias_overall)) {
    z_overall_mean <- round(mean(bias_overall$z_mean, na.rm = TRUE), 2)
    z_overall_q2.5 <- round(mean(bias_overall$z_q2.5, na.rm = TRUE), 2)
    z_overall_q97.5 <- round(mean(bias_overall$z_q97.5, na.rm = TRUE), 2)
  }
}
```

## Bias and Phasic Arousal

The null effect of effort on starting-point bias (H4) suggests that concurrent handgrip at 40% MVC did not reset or neutralize pre-existing response preferences in older adults. Starting-point bias was consistently above 0.5 across conditions ($z = `r z_overall_mean`$, 95% CrI [`r z_overall_q2.5`, `r z_overall_q97.5`]; @tbl-standard-only-bias-levels), indicating a systematic tendency toward "different" responses that effort did not attenuate.

Critically, this pattern reflects a **liberal** response bias in Signal Detection Theory terms — participants were predisposed to report "Different" with relatively low evidentiary thresholds. This contrasts with the conservative recognition criterion (high $\beta$, reflected in a response bias *away* from "old" or "signal") typically reported in older adults in episodic recognition memory tasks [@koen2016]. The present paradigm is a change-detection task, not a recognition memory task, and the "Different" response corresponds to detecting a *signal* (a change is present). A starting point biased toward "Different" therefore reflects a liberal detection strategy — more false alarms, fewer misses — not a conservative one.

The liberal detection strategy is consistent with the "Different-as-default heuristic" documented in same-different paradigms [@farell1985; @nosofsky1997palmeri]: detecting any mismatch is self-terminating (the comparison can stop at the first discrepant feature), whereas confirming sameness requires exhaustive feature comparison. Under concurrent grip load at 40% MVC, adopting a liberal "Different" starting point reduces the cognitive expense of Standard (Same) trials at the cost of reduced discrimination accuracy — a sensible tradeoff when both arousal and response-time pressure are elevated. The stability of this liberal bias across effort conditions (null H4 effect) further suggests it reflects a deeply habituated task strategy rather than a state-dependent adjustment to momentary arousal.

This contrasts with prior work showing that pupil-indexed phasic arousal can shift response criterion in younger adults [@degee2020pupil], and may reflect an age-related reduction in the efficacy of phasic LC-NE signals to modulate criterion setting dynamically [@huang2024]. As noted in Section 3.6, the unexpected reversal of TEPR magnitude across effort conditions (@tbl-tepr) suggests that our pupil measure may have been compromised by motor-autonomic confounds inherent to the sustained grip manipulation, limiting our ability to detect genuine arousal-parameter coupling even if present. Importantly, a robust *task-level* bias difference was observed: older adults showed a stronger tendency toward *different* responses in the ADT compared to the VDT ($\Delta z = -0.04$, 95% CrI [−0.06, −0.02]; @tbl-standard-only-bias-contrasts). This task asymmetry likely reflects the inherent perceptual asymmetry of the auditory change-detection task, where frequency offsets create a more salient "different" signal relative to the subtler luminance contrast changes in the VDT. The bias difference was not modulated by effort in either task, suggesting it reflects a stable perceptual tendency rather than a state-dependent strategic adjustment. Future work examining whether LC integrity moderates this task-specific liberal bias — particularly given the LC's role in sensory gating [@mather2016; @huang2024] — would be informative.

## Limitations and Future Directions

Several limitations constrain the interpretation of these findings. First, the standard Wiener DDM assumes constant drift within each trial and does not include across-trial variability in drift ($s_v$), starting point ($s_z$), or non-decision time ($s_{t_0}$). This produced localized fast-tail misfit, most pronounced in Easy VDT conditions, where the model underpredicted the frequency of very fast correct responses — likely reflecting a subset of anticipatory responses or an extremely high-drift regime incompatible with the Wiener process at the cell level. Sensitivity analyses using 2% fast-response censoring and visual inspection of mid-body quantile-probability plots confirmed that this misfit did not alter the direction or credibility of any key parameter contrast (Appendix A3). Future extensions incorporating across-trial variability, a fast-guess contaminant mixture, or urgency-collapsing boundaries may improve absolute fit, particularly for Easy trials [@ratcliff2008diffusion].

Second, the response-signal paradigm imposes structural constraints on parameter estimation. Because the response window is externally gated, non-decision time $t_0$ could not be estimated with condition-specific variation without instability (see Section 2.3.2 and the H3 discussion above), limiting the direct test of H3. Reaction times are measured from response-screen onset rather than stimulus onset, confining the interpretation of $t_0$ to motor execution and response selection rather than early perceptual encoding. These design choices were necessary given the MRI-compatible grip-force paradigm but limit generalizability to free-response paradigms where $t_0$ reflects the full encoding-decision-motor chain.

Third, the trial-wise pupil predictor (W3.0 AUC) spans both pre- and post-response epochs, making it difficult to isolate phasic arousal during evidence accumulation from post-decisional pupil dynamics. Although RT was included as a covariate in all pupil-DDM models to partial out response-timing confounds, we did not test sensitivity to AUC window definition (e.g., a pre-response W1.3 window). Additionally, PSIS-LOO estimates for pupil-augmented models were unreliable (Pareto-$k > 0.7$), so model comparison was limited; conclusions about pupil effects are based on posterior coefficient distributions rather than LOO-based model selection [@vehtari2017loo].

Fourth, the concurrent isometric handgrip manipulation (40% MVC) may interact with motor execution in ways not fully captured by small fixed effects on $t_0$; future work integrating EMG or kinematic measures could disentangle central resource competition from peripheral motor interference. Linear Ballistic Accumulator or race models may also better accommodate the fast-tail RT dynamics observed in Easy-difficulty conditions, and future work could explore whether these model families yield the same substantive pattern of effort and difficulty effects on decision parameters.


## Conclusions

This chapter establishes that effort-induced arousal degrades evidence accumulation quality — not response caution or peripheral processing speed — in older adults. The DDM decomposition provides the mechanistic specificity that traditional RT-accuracy analyses cannot offer: the 40% MVC handgrip cost is localized to the drift rate parameter $v$, implicating the signal-to-noise ratio of perceptual evidence accumulation as the proximal target of effort-induced interference. The null effects on boundary separation and non-decision time further narrow the theoretical account, ruling out strategic caution adjustment and peripheral motor slowing as primary mechanisms. These findings set the stage for Chapter 4, which directly tests whether locus coeruleus–norepinephrine (LC-NE) integrity — quantified via neuromelanin-sensitive MRI — moderates the effort-induced drift rate reduction observed here, and whether individuals with higher LC integrity are buffered against the perceptual costs of high physical demand.

```{r}
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.3), size = 0.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Cue-locked" = "#2E86AB", "Probe-onset-locked" = "#A23B72"), name = "RT Definition") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Baseline" = 17, "Additive" = 19), guide = "none") +
  labs(
    x = "Model",
    y = "LOOIC (lower is better)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

print(p_loo)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-convergence-ppc-gate-appendix
#| tbl-cap: "Convergence and PPC Diagnostics (Primary Model). Convergence criteria (R-hat, ESS, divergences) were strictly satisfied (PASS). PPC metrics show exceedances of pre-registered strict thresholds, driven by fast-tail misfit — a known limitation of standard Wiener DDM without fast-guess processes. These PPC threshold failures do not invalidate parameter contrasts; visual diagnostics (QP plots, Appendix A3.2) confirmed adequate mid-body fit, and key contrasts were robust to tail deviations. Note: 'Convergence verdict' and 'PPC verdict' reflect different standards — convergence is a binary prerequisite for valid inference; PPC threshold failures indicate model limitations but do not prevent interpretation. See Section 3.2 and Appendix A3 for full discussion."
#| tbl-pos: "htbp"
# Prefer run_dir convergence (matches main DDM data); fallback to publish_gate for conv and PPC
conv_primary_row <- tbl_convergence %>%
  filter(model == PRIMARY_MODEL, rt_type == PRIMARY_RT, threshold == PRIMARY_THR) %>%
  slice(1)
conv_max_rhat   <- if (nrow(conv_primary_row) > 0) conv_primary_row$max_rhat   else (if (!is.null(publish_gate)) publish_gate$conv_max_rhat   else NA_real_)
conv_min_bulk   <- if (nrow(conv_primary_row) > 0) conv_primary_row$min_bulk_ess else (if (!is.null(publish_gate)) publish_gate$conv_min_bulk_ess else NA_real_)
conv_min_tail   <- if (!is.null(publish_gate) && !is.na(publish_gate$conv_min_tail_ess)) publish_gate$conv_min_tail_ess else NA_real_  # run_dir has no tail ESS
conv_div        <- if (nrow(conv_primary_row) > 0) conv_primary_row$n_divergent else (if (!is.null(publish_gate)) publish_gate$conv_divergences else NA_integer_)
conv_pass       <- !is.na(conv_max_rhat) && conv_max_rhat < 1.01 && !is.na(conv_min_bulk) && conv_min_bulk >= 400 && !is.na(conv_div) && conv_div == 0
ppc_n_cells     <- if (!is.null(publish_gate)) publish_gate$ppc_subj_n_cells     else NA_real_
ppc_pct_flagged <- if (!is.null(publish_gate)) publish_gate$ppc_subj_pct_flagged_any else NA_real_
ppc_max_qp      <- if (!is.null(publish_gate)) publish_gate$ppc_subj_max_qp     else NA_real_
ppc_max_ks      <- if (!is.null(publish_gate)) publish_gate$ppc_subj_max_ks      else NA_real_
ppc_pass        <- if (!is.null(publish_gate)) publish_gate$ppc_subj_pass        else NA
if (!is.null(publish_gate) || nrow(conv_primary_row) > 0) {
  gate_tbl <- tibble(
    Metric = c(
      "Max R-hat", "Min Bulk ESS", "Min Tail ESS", "Divergences",
      "Convergence verdict", "PPC Cells (n)", "PPC Flagged (%)",
      "Max QP RMSE (s)", "Max KS", "PPC verdict"
    ),
    Value = c(
      ifelse(is.na(conv_max_rhat), "—", sprintf("%.4f", conv_max_rhat)),
      ifelse(is.na(conv_min_bulk), "—", sprintf("%.0f", conv_min_bulk)),
      ifelse(is.na(conv_min_tail), "—", sprintf("%.0f", conv_min_tail)),
      as.character(ifelse(is.na(conv_div), "—", conv_div)),
      ifelse(is.na(conv_pass), "—", ifelse(conv_pass, "PASS (Rhat ≤ 1.01, ESS ≥ 400, 0 divergences)", "FAIL")),
      ifelse(is.na(ppc_n_cells), "—", sprintf("%.0f", ppc_n_cells)),
      ifelse(is.na(ppc_pct_flagged), "—", sprintf("%.1f%%", ppc_pct_flagged)),
      ifelse(is.na(ppc_max_qp), "—", sprintf("%.3f", ppc_max_qp)),
      ifelse(is.na(ppc_max_ks), "—", sprintf("%.3f", ppc_max_ks)),
      ifelse(is.na(ppc_pass), "—", ifelse(ppc_pass, "PASS strict thresholds", "FAIL pre-registered thresholds (fast-tail driven; mid-body fit adequate, inferences robust)"))
    )
  )
  gate_tbl %>% gt() %>%
    tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"), locations = cells_column_labels()) %>%
    tab_style(style = cell_text(style = "italic"), locations = cells_body(columns = Metric)) %>%
    cols_width(Metric ~ px(180), Value ~ px(100)) %>% opt_table_font(size = "small")
} else {
  invisible(NULL)
}
```

## A2. Individual Differences and Parameter Relationships {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| label: fig-subject-parameter-distribution
#| fig-cap: "Subject-Level Parameter Distribution. Violin plots showing the distribution of subject-level random effects (deviations from group mean) for each DDM parameter. The boxplots within each violin show the median and interquartile range. Zero (dashed line) represents the group mean. This visualization highlights the substantial individual variability in decision-making parameters across our sample of 67 older adults."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: "htbp"
#| out-width: "75%"
# Dynamic: from model ranef when brms available
model_path_re <- file.path(proj_root, params$run_dir, "models", "additive__probe_onset_locked__thr0.20.rds")
if (file.exists(model_path_re) && requireNamespace("brms", quietly = TRUE)) {
  tryCatch({
    suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(brms))
    fit_re <- readRDS(model_path_re)
    re <- ranef(fit_re)
    if (!is.null(re) && "subject_id" %in% names(re)) {
      re_subj <- re$subject_id
      par_names <- dimnames(re_subj)[[3]]
      re_list <- list()
      for (par in par_names) {
        if ("Estimate" %in% dimnames(re_subj)[[2]]) {
          re_est <- re_subj[, "Estimate", par]
          re_list[[length(re_list) + 1]] <- tibble(subject_id = names(re_est), parameter = par, estimate = as.numeric(re_est))
        }
      }
      if (length(re_list) > 0) {
      re_df <- bind_rows(re_list) %>%
        mutate(
          parameter = case_when(
            parameter == "Intercept" | (grepl("Intercept", parameter) & !grepl("bias|bs|ndt", parameter)) ~ "Drift (v)",
            grepl("bs_|boundary", parameter, ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "Boundary (a)",
            grepl("bias", parameter, ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "Bias (z)",
            grepl("ndt", parameter, ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "Non-decision time (t0)",
            TRUE ~ parameter
          )
        )
      re_df$parameter <- factor(re_df$parameter, levels = c("Drift (v)", "Boundary (a)", "Bias (z)", "Non-decision time (t0)"))
      re_df <- re_df %>% filter(!is.na(parameter))
      if (nrow(re_df) > 0) {
        p_re <- ggplot(re_df, aes(x = parameter, y = estimate, fill = parameter)) +
          geom_violin(alpha = 0.3, trim = FALSE) +
          geom_boxplot(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.7, outlier.shape = NA) +
          geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50", linewidth = 0.5) +
          scale_fill_manual(values = c("Drift (v)" = "#2E86AB", "Boundary (a)" = "#A23B72", "Bias (z)" = "#28A745", "Non-decision time (t0)" = "#6C757D"), guide = "none") +
          labs(title = "Subject-Level Parameter Estimates (Random Effects)", subtitle = "Individual differences in DDM parameters",
               x = "DDM Parameter", y = "Random Effect Estimate (link scale)", fill = "Parameter") +
          theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
          theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5), legend.position = "none", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
        print(p_re)
      } else { include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_subject_parameter_distribution.pdf")) }
      } else { include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_subject_parameter_distribution.pdf")) }
    } else { include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_subject_parameter_distribution.pdf")) }
  }, error = function(e) { include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_subject_parameter_distribution.pdf")) })
} else {
include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_subject_parameter_distribution.pdf"))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-parameter-correlation
#| fig-cap: "Subject-Level Parameter Correlation: Drift Intercept vs. Bias Intercept. Scatter plot showing the relationship between subject-level random-effect estimates for drift intercept and bias intercept. Each point represents one participant ($n$ = 67). The correlation is $r$ = −0.205, indicating a weak negative association; participants with stronger negative drift tend to show slightly lower starting-point bias. The regression line with 95% confidence band is shown."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: "htbp"
#| out-width: "70%"
# Dynamic: from model coef when brms available
model_path_cor <- file.path(proj_root, params$run_dir, "models", "additive__probe_onset_locked__thr0.20.rds")
if (file.exists(model_path_cor) && requireNamespace("brms", quietly = TRUE)) {
  tryCatch({
    suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(brms))
    fit_cor <- readRDS(model_path_cor)
    coef_subj <- coef(fit_cor, summary = TRUE)
    if (!is.null(coef_subj) && "subject_id" %in% names(coef_subj)) {
      drift_coefs <- coef_subj$subject_id[, , "Intercept"]
      bias_coefs <- coef_subj$subject_id[, , "bias_Intercept"]
      if (!is.null(drift_coefs) && !is.null(bias_coefs)) {
        subj_cor <- tibble(subject_id = rownames(drift_coefs), drift_intercept = drift_coefs[, "Estimate"], bias_intercept = bias_coefs[, "Estimate"])
        cor_val <- cor(subj_cor$drift_intercept, subj_cor$bias_intercept, use = "complete.obs")
        p_cor <- ggplot(subj_cor, aes(x = drift_intercept, y = bias_intercept)) +
          geom_point(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.7, color = "#1f78b4") +
          geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "#DC143C", linewidth = 0.8, fill = "gray90", alpha = 0.3) +
          labs(title = "Subject-Level Parameter Correlation", subtitle = sprintf("Drift Intercept vs. Bias Intercept (r = %.3f)", cor_val),
               x = "Drift Intercept (Subject-Level)", y = "Bias Intercept (Subject-Level, logit scale)") +
          theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
          theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5), plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5, color = "gray50"))
        print(p_cor)
      } else { include_graphics_safe(fig_path("plot4_parameter_correlation.png")) }
    } else { include_graphics_safe(fig_path("plot4_parameter_correlation.png")) }
  }, error = function(e) { include_graphics_safe(fig_path("plot4_parameter_correlation.png")) })
} else {
include_graphics_safe(fig_path("plot4_parameter_correlation.png"))
}
```
